extracted.intended_audience: Princeton community and general public interested in mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: A university press/news obituary announcing a scholar's death that summarizes biography, major contributions, honors, personal anecdotes, memorial arrangements, and contact/share information for the community. Aimed at informing and commemorating for both specialist and general audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Death announcement details
rubrics_metrics.description: John Horton Conway... died on Saturday, April 11, in New Brunswick, New Jersey, from complications related to COVID-19. He was 82.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead should state clearly that the subject has died and include date, place, cause (if appropriate), and age to orient readers immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memorial/visitation information
rubrics_metrics.description: A memorial/visitation honoring Conway will be held Sunday, Oct. 11, from 3-5 p.m., at Mather-Hodge Funeral Home, 40 Vandeventer Ave., Princeton, NJ 08542. The visitation will be from 3-4 p.m.; friends will be invited to speak from 4-5 p.m. Social distancing regulations limit the number of people inside at one time to 25. Please wear a face covering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide practical event details (date, time, location, schedule of events) and any public-health or attendance restrictions and recommended precautions. Be specific about visitation vs ceremony times and any RSVP/contact requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact information for questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions may be directed to dianaconway13@aol.com.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a contact (email or phone) for inquiries about memorials, further information, or media questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic positions and titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Conway, who joined the faculty in 1987, was the John von Neumann Professor in Applied and Computational Mathematics and a professor of mathematics until 2013 when he transferred to emeritus status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List institutional appointments, named chairs, and emeritus status with dates where relevant to establish the subject's official roles and standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photo with credit
rubrics_metrics.description: John Horton Conway Photo by Denise Applewhite, Office of Communications
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include an accompanying photograph and clearly attribute the photographer and office. Photo credit and source should be visible and accurate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colleague quotations illustrating impact
rubrics_metrics.description: "John Conway was an amazing mathematician, game wizard, polymath and storyteller who left an indelible mark..." — Igor Rodnianski; other quotes from Simon Kochen, Peter Doyle, David Gabai, Peter Sarnak, Joseph Kohn, Diana Conway, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate multiple short quotes from colleagues, collaborators, and family to convey the subject's personality, influence, and the community's reaction. Use quotes that highlight character, teaching style, and scientific contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary of contributions and fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Over his long career, Conway made significant contributions to mathematics in the fields of group theory, number theory, algebra, geometric topology, theoretical physics, combinatorial game theory and geometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a concise listing of the major fields and areas where the subject made contributions to give readers a sense of breadth and scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description of notable works and inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: One of Conway's most well-known accomplishments was the Game of Life... The achievement for which Conway himself was most proud... was his invention of a new system of numbers, the surreal numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe signature achievements (e.g., inventions, theorems, games) with brief explanations of what they are, their origins, and why they matter. Contextualize for non-specialist readers (history, relation to other work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Description of specific research results and implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Later, with Kochen, Conway developed and proved the Free Will Theorem in 2004... In number theory, Conway proved... that every integer could be written as the sum of 37 numbers, each raised to the fifth power. In 1993... he proved... an integral positive definite quadratic form... represents all positive integers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include representative technical results with a plain-language explanation of their content and significance or implications so readers can appreciate specific scholarly impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honors and awards
rubrics_metrics.description: Conway’s numerous honors include the London Mathematical Society’s Berwick Prize and Pólya Prize, Northwestern University’s Nemmers Prize in Mathematics, and the American Mathematical Society’s Leroy P. Steele Prize for Mathematical Exposition. Conway is a fellow of the Royal Society of London and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List major prizes, fellowships, memberships in learned societies, and other formal recognitions to document peer recognition and prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and career timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Conway was born in Liverpool, England, on December 26, 1937. He received his B.A. from Cambridge University in 1959 and his Ph.D. from the same institution in 1964. He was a faculty member at Cambridge until he came to Princeton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide birthplace, birthdate, degrees (institutions and years), and principal academic appointments in chronological order to chart the subject's career path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal anecdotes and character details
rubrics_metrics.description: Conway often carried in his pockets props such as ropes, pennies, cards, dice, models and sometimes a Slinky... His regular office was filled to overflowing with books and colorful toy models... 'Once he shook my hand and informed me that I was four handshakes away from Napoleon...' (anecdote from Gabai).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include vivid, humanizing anecdotes and small stories that reveal personality, teaching style, and habits; these make the piece engaging and memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survivors and family information
rubrics_metrics.description: Conway is survived by Diana Conway and son Gareth. He is also survived by sons Alex and Oliver from his second marriage... and daughters Susie, Rosie, Ellie and Annie from his first marriage... also survived by three grandchildren and six great-grandchildren.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List immediate surviving family members by name and relation. Include spouses, children, grandchildren as appropriate to inform readers and for condolences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Links to related stories and ways to share or comment
rubrics_metrics.description: View or share comments on a blog intended to honor Conway’s life and legacy. Related Stories (links to other news items).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide links to a memorial or comment page, and related stories for readers who want more background or to participate in remembrance. Offer clear navigation to further reading.
